subject: chemistry
pattern: One of the highest-weight organic chapters in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper, about 10-12 marks: a 1-mark named reaction (Rosenmund, Etard) or IUPAC name, 2-mark Cannizzaro/Clemmensen/HVZ or reasoning questions, a 3-mark distinguishing test or aldol mechanism, and a 5-mark question on preparation or reactions of aldehydes, ketones or carboxylic acids. Examiners look for reagents above arrows, correct products and the reason for reactivity (aldehyde more reactive than ketone, acidity trends).

questions.q: What is Rosenmund reduction? Give the equation.
questions.answer: Acyl chloride is hydrogenated over palladium catalysed on barium sulphate (poisoned catalyst) to give the aldehyde. CH$_3$COCl + H$_2$ → (Pd-BaSO$_4$) CH$_3$CHO + HCl. The poison prevents further reduction of the aldehyde to alcohol.

questions.q: What is Etard reaction? Write the equation.
questions.answer: Toluene is oxidised with chromyl chloride (CrO$_2$Cl$_2$) in CS$_2$ to form a chromium complex, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde. C$_6$H$_5$CH$_3$ + CrO$_2$Cl$_2$ → chromium complex → (H$_3$O$^+$) C$_6$H$_5$CHO.

questions.q: Write the IUPAC names of (i) CH$_3$-CO-CH$_2$CH$_2$CH$_3$ (ii) HOOC-CH$_2$-COOH (iii) CH$_3$CH(CH$_3$)CHO.
questions.answer: (i) Pentan-2-one (five-carbon chain, C=O at carbon 2). (ii) Propanedioic acid (common name malonic acid). (iii) 2-Methylpropanal (three-carbon chain, methyl on carbon 2, -CHO is carbon 1).

questions.q: Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than alcohols of comparable molecular mass. Why?
questions.answer: Carboxylic acids form extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds. In the pure liquid or in the vapour of non-polar solvents, two molecules join through two hydrogen bonds to give a stable cyclic dimer. Such dimerisation doubles the effective molecular mass and the hydrogen bonds are stronger than those in alcohols (the O-H bond is more polarised), so more energy is required to separate the molecules. Hence carboxylic acids boil at a higher temperature than alcohols.

questions.q: What is Cannizzaro reaction? Give an example.
questions.answer: Aldehydes that have no alpha-hydrogen atom, when heated with concentrated alkali, undergo self oxidation-reduction (disproportionation): one molecule is oxidised to carboxylate salt and another is reduced to alcohol. 2HCHO + conc. NaOH → CH$_3$OH + HCOONa. Similarly 2C$_6$H$_5$CHO + conc. NaOH → C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$OH + C$_6$H$_5$COONa.

questions.q: Explain Clemmensen reduction and Wolff-Kishner reduction with equations.
questions.answer: Both convert the carbonyl group (C=O) to a methylene group (CH$_2$). Clemmensen reduction: the aldehyde or ketone is heated with zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl. C=O + Zn-Hg/conc. HCl → CH$_2$ (e.g. CH$_3$COCH$_3$ → CH$_3$CH$_2$CH$_3$). Wolff-Kishner reduction: the carbonyl compound is first converted into hydrazone with hydrazine, then heated with KOH or NaOH in ethylene glycol at high temperature. C=O + NH$_2$NH$_2$ → C=NNH$_2$ → (KOH, ethylene glycol, heat) CH$_2$ + N$_2$.

questions.q: What is Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction? Give the equation.
questions.answer: Carboxylic acids having an alpha-hydrogen are halogenated at the alpha-position on treatment with chlorine or bromine in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus, to give alpha-halocarboxylic acids. R-CH$_2$-COOH + X$_2$ → (red P) R-CHX-COOH + HX. Example: CH$_3$COOH + Cl$_2$ → (red P) ClCH$_2$COOH.

questions.q: How will you distinguish between (i) ethanal and propanone (ii) benzaldehyde and acetophenone (iii) pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one?
questions.answer: (i) Ethanal reduces Tollens' reagent giving a silver mirror and Fehling's solution giving a red precipitate of Cu$_2$O; propanone does not. (ii) Acetophenone (a methyl ketone) gives yellow precipitate of iodoform (CHI$_3$) with NaOI (I$_2$/NaOH); benzaldehyde does not (it gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, acetophenone does not). (iii) Pentan-2-one contains the CH$_3$CO- group and gives iodoform test (yellow precipitate); pentan-3-one does not.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group. Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition?
questions.answer: The carbonyl carbon is sp$^2$ hybridised and electrophilic because oxygen is more electronegative. The nucleophile (Nu$^-$) attacks the carbon from above or below the plane of the molecule; the pi electrons shift to oxygen forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which takes a proton to give the product. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because (1) steric factor: aldehydes have only one alkyl group (and one small H), so the attack is easier, but ketones have two bulky alkyl groups causing hindrance; (2) electronic factor: two +I alkyl groups in ketones reduce the positive charge on carbonyl carbon more than the single alkyl group in aldehydes.

questions.q: Explain aldol condensation with mechanism, taking ethanal as example.
questions.answer: Aldehydes and ketones having alpha-hydrogen, in the presence of dilute alkali, give beta-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols) which on heating lose water to form alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compounds. Step 1: OH$^-$ removes an alpha-hydrogen from CH$_3$CHO to form the enolate carbanion -CH$_2$CHO. Step 2: the carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon of another ethanal molecule to form an alkoxide, which takes H$^+$ from water to form aldol, CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_2$CHO (3-hydroxybutanal). Step 3: on heating, dehydration gives but-2-enal, CH$_3$CH=CHCHO.

questions.q: Arrange in the increasing order of acidic strength and explain: formic acid, acetic acid, chloroacetic acid, benzoic acid. How do electron-withdrawing and electron-donating groups affect acid strength?
questions.answer: Increasing acidity: acetic acid (pKa 4.76) < benzoic acid (4.19) < formic acid (3.75) < chloroacetic acid (2.86). Electron-withdrawing groups (-Cl, -NO$_2$, -CN) disperse the negative charge of the carboxylate ion by -I effect, stabilising it and increasing acidity; more such groups and nearer to the COOH group give greater acidity. Electron-donating groups (alkyl, +I) intensify the negative charge on the carboxylate ion, destabilise it and decrease acidity. Hence acetic acid is weaker than formic acid. Phenyl group is electron withdrawing (sp$^2$ carbon), so benzoic acid is stronger than acetic acid.

questions.q: Give the chemical tests to distinguish between carboxylic acid and phenol, and between formic acid and acetic acid.
questions.answer: Carboxylic acid vs phenol: carboxylic acids liberate brisk effervescence of CO$_2$ with sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO$_3$) solution since they are stronger acids than carbonic acid; phenol does not. Phenol gives violet colour with neutral FeCl$_3$ solution; carboxylic acids (except some) do not. Formic acid vs acetic acid: formic acid has an aldehyde group and so reduces Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's solution (red precipitate) and decolourises acidified KMnO$_4$; acetic acid does not give these tests.

questions.q: Explain with equations any five methods of preparation of aldehydes and ketones.
questions.answer: (1) Oxidation of primary alcohols (to aldehydes) with PCC, and of secondary alcohols (to ketones) with CrO$_3$ or K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$. (2) Dehydrogenation: alcohol vapour passed over hot Cu at 573 K gives aldehyde or ketone: CH$_3$CH$_2$OH → CH$_3$CHO + H$_2$. (3) Hydration of alkynes: ethyne + H$_2$O/HgSO$_4$/H$_2$SO$_4$ → ethanal; propyne gives propanone. (4) Rosenmund reduction of acyl chloride (aldehydes): RCOCl + H$_2$/Pd-BaSO$_4$ → RCHO. (5) Stephen reaction: nitrile + SnCl$_2$/HCl, then H$_3$O$^+$ → aldehyde. (6) Nitrile + Grignard reagent then hydrolysis gives ketone; acyl chloride + dialkylcadmium gives ketone. (7) Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with acetyl chloride/anhyd. AlCl$_3$ gives acetophenone. (8) Etard reaction gives benzaldehyde.

questions.q: Explain the following reactions of aldehydes and ketones with equations: (i) addition of HCN (ii) reaction with 2,4-DNP (iii) Tollens' test (iv) Fehling's test (v) iodoform reaction.
questions.answer: (i) HCN adds to C=O to form cyanohydrin: CH$_3$CHO + HCN → CH$_3$CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile). (ii) With 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, the carbonyl compound gives yellow-orange 2,4-DNP derivative (hydrazone), used for identification. (iii) Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO$_3$) is reduced by aldehydes to silver mirror: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH$_3$)$_2$]$^+$ + 3OH$^-$ → RCOO$^-$ + 2Ag + 2H$_2$O + 4NH$_3$. (iv) Fehling's solution (alkaline Cu$^{2+}$ tartrate) is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes to red precipitate of Cu$_2$O; aromatic aldehydes do not respond. (v) Aldehydes and ketones with CH$_3$CO- group (and CH$_3$CH(OH)- alcohols) give yellow precipitate of iodoform on warming with NaOH and I$_2$: CH$_3$COCH$_3$ + 3I$_2$ + 4NaOH → CHI$_3$ + CH$_3$COONa + 3NaI + 3H$_2$O.

questions.q: Explain with equations five methods of preparation and any three chemical reactions of carboxylic acids.
questions.answer: Preparation: (1) oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes with KMnO$_4$ or K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$: RCH$_2$OH → RCOOH. (2) Hydrolysis of nitriles: RCN + H$_2$O/H$^+$ → RCOOH + NH$_4$$^+$. (3) Grignard reagent with CO$_2$, followed by acid hydrolysis: RMgX + CO$_2$ → RCOOMgX → RCOOH. (4) Hydrolysis of esters or acyl chlorides/anhydrides. (5) Oxidation of alkylbenzenes with KMnO$_4$ gives benzoic acid. Reactions: (a) with PCl$_5$/SOCl$_2$ gives acyl chloride; (b) esterification with alcohol/conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ gives ester; (c) reduction with LiAlH$_4$ or B$_2$H$_6$ gives primary alcohol; also reacts with NaHCO$_3$ liberating CO$_2$, and heating the sodium salt with soda lime gives alkane (decarboxylation).
